Number System, LCM & HCF

Almost every CUET Numerical Ability section opens with 1-2 number-system questions: classifying numbers, divisibility rules, or an LCM/HCF word problem. These are pure speed points if the rules are automatic.

Start here

What Number System, LCM and HCF are about

Number System is the grammar of arithmetic. It tells you what kinds of numbers exist (natural, whole, integers, primes, composites, rationals), how they behave when divided, and how to find the numbers that divide, or are divisible by, several numbers at once (HCF and LCM).

CUET questions here are short: apply a divisibility test, find an HCF or LCM, use a remainder fact, or count factors. Once the rules are automatic, each question takes under 40 seconds.

In depth

The ideas behind the topic, explained

Why prime factorisation is the master key

Every whole number above 1 is a product of primes in exactly one way. Writing 360 as 2³ × 3² × 5 turns three different questions into one job: its HCF with another number, its LCM, and its number of factors all read straight off the exponents. Whenever two numbers are given, factorise both before doing anything else.

How divisibility tests really work

Our number system is built on powers of 10. Since 10 leaves remainder 1 when divided by 3 or 9, every digit contributes only itself, so the digit sum decides divisibility by 3 and 9. For 11, place values alternate between remainder +1 and −1, which is why the difference of alternate digit sums is used. For 4 and 8, 100 and 1,000 are already multiples, so only the last two or three digits matter.

HCF versus LCM in everyday words

HCF answers 'the biggest piece that fits exactly into every length', such as the largest tile or the greatest number of equal groups. LCM answers 'when do repeating events meet again', such as bells ringing together, or the smallest quantity that can be packed in several ways. One goes down to a common divisor, the other goes up to a common multiple.

The tricks

9 tricks, and why each one works

A trick you only memorise fails under pressure. Each one comes with its reason, so you can rebuild it if you forget it. Tap a trick to open it.

1Use the digit sum for 3 and 9

Add the digits. If the sum is divisible by 3 the number is; if it is divisible by 9 the number is divisible by 9.

Why it worksEvery place value (10, 100, 1000 ...) leaves remainder 1 when divided by 9, so a number behaves like its digit sum.

2'Largest' means HCF, 'smallest' means LCM

Largest number that divides all: HCF. Smallest number divisible by all: LCM.

Why it worksHCF is never larger than the smallest number given; LCM is never smaller than the largest. 'Divides' and 'divisible by' point in opposite directions.

3Remainder trick: LCM plus the common remainder

If N leaves remainder r with divisors a, b, c, then N = LCM(a,b,c) × k + r.

Why it worksN − r is divisible by every divisor, so N − r is a multiple of the LCM.

4When the gap is common, subtract it

If each remainder is 1 less than its divisor, N = LCM × k − 1.

Why it worksThen N + 1 is divisible by every divisor, so N + 1 is a multiple of the LCM.

5Count factors from the primes

Write N as p^a × q^b × r^c. Factors = (a+1)(b+1)(c+1).

Why it worksEach factor picks a power of p from 0 to a, of q from 0 to b, and so on; the choices multiply.

6Verify with HCF × LCM

For two numbers, HCF × LCM must equal their product.

Why it worksEach prime appears once at its lowest power (in HCF) and once at its highest (in LCM), so together they give both exponents.

7Co-prime numbers have HCF 1

If two numbers share no prime factor, their LCM is simply their product.

Why it worksWith no common prime, the product already contains every prime of each number exactly once.

8Largest divisor that leaves given remainders

To find the largest number dividing a, b and c leaving remainders r₁, r₂, r₃, take the HCF of (a − r₁), (b − r₂), (c − r₃).

Why it worksSubtracting the remainders makes each number exactly divisible by the required divisor.

9Test a prime only up to its square root

To test 91, test primes up to 9: 7 divides it (7 × 13).

Why it worksIf a number has a factor larger than its square root, it must also have one smaller than its square root.

One-line method
Classify the number → choose the rule → prime-factorise → lowest powers for HCF, highest for LCM → verify with HCF × LCM.
Solved examples

6 solved examples, from easy to tricky

The numbered circles in the question line match the red-pen steps below it.

Example 1 · Divisibility
Test whether 4,572 is divisible by 9 using the digit sum
1Add the digits: 4 + 5 + 7 + 2 = 18.
218 is divisible by 9, so the whole number is.
4,572 is divisible by 9 (and therefore also by 3).
Example 2 · HCF and LCM
Find the HCF and LCM of 24 and 36
124 = 2³ × 3 and 36 = 2² × 3². Common primes at the lowest power: 2² × 3 = 12.
2Highest powers: 2³ and 3², giving 8 × 9 = 72. Check: 12 × 72 = 864 = 24 × 36.
HCF = 12, LCM = 72.
Example 3 · Largest tile
A room 8 m 40 cm long and 6 m 30 cm wide is tiled with square tiles. Find the largest tile
1Convert to one unit: 840 cm and 630 cm. 'Largest square tile that fits exactly' means HCF.
2840 = 2³·3·5·7 and 630 = 2·3²·5·7. HCF = 2·3·5·7 = 210.
The largest tile has a side of 210 cm.
Example 4 · Remainder
Find the smallest number that leaves remainder 3 when divided by 4, 6 and 8
1N − 3 must be divisible by 4, 6 and 8, so it is a multiple of LCM(4, 6, 8).
2LCM = 24, so the smallest N is 24 + 3.
N = 27.
Example 5 · Common-gap trap
Find the smallest number which leaves remainder 4 when divided by 5 and remainder 6 when divided by 7
1Each remainder is 1 less than its divisor, so N + 1 is divisible by both 5 and 7.
2LCM(5, 7) = 35, so N + 1 = 35 and N = 34.
N = 34. Check: 34 = 5×6 + 4 = 7×4 + 6.
Example 6 · Largest divisor with remainders
Find the largest number that divides 60 and 75 leaving remainders 4 and 5
1Subtract the remainders: 60 − 4 = 56 and 75 − 5 = 70.
2The number must divide both 56 and 70, so take their HCF: 56 = 2³·7 and 70 = 2·5·7, giving HCF = 14.
The largest such number is 14. Check: 60 = 14 × 4 + 4 and 75 = 14 × 5 + 5.

Simplification, Approximation & Surds

Simplification tests BODMAS discipline under time pressure; approximation questions reward rounding smartly instead of calculating exactly — a critical speed skill for a timed exam.

Start here

What Simplification, Approximation and Surds are about

Simplification means reducing a long expression with brackets, fractions, powers and roots to one value by obeying the order of operations. Approximation means getting a value close enough to pick the correct option by rounding smartly. Surds are roots that do not come out as whole numbers, such as √2 or √3.

These are speed questions. The marks go to the student who follows BODMAS without slipping and who knows when an exact calculation is not needed.

In depth

The ideas behind the topic, explained

Why the order of operations exists

Mathematics needs one agreed order so that an expression has exactly one value. Brackets override everything because they group what belongs together. 'Of' binds a fraction to its object, powers and roots act on a single number, and only then do multiplication and division, then addition and subtraction, combine results. Without this agreement, 8 + 2 × 5 could be read as 18 or as 50.

Left to right inside the same rank

Division and multiplication share a rank, as do addition and subtraction, so inside a rank you simply work from left to right. For 24 ÷ 4 × 3 the answer is 6 × 3 = 18, not 24 ÷ 12 = 2. Learners who treat 'D then M' as strict priorities get this wrong.

When rounding is safe in approximation

Approximation questions give options that are spread apart, so each number can be rounded to the nearest convenient value. Round to one or two significant digits, note whether you rounded up or down, and prefer numbers that divide easily, such as 25, 50, 100 or 1,000. Do not round when the options are close together.

The tricks

9 tricks, and why each one works

A trick you only memorise fails under pressure. Each one comes with its reason, so you can rebuild it if you forget it. Tap a trick to open it.

1Work from the innermost bracket outward

Rewrite the expression after each step. Never do two operations at once.

Why it worksSkipping lines is how order and sign errors enter, and a wrong value earns no marks however fast it was found.

2'Of' is multiplication that goes first

In '¼ of 40 + 6', do ¼ of 40 = 10 first, then add 6.

Why it works'Of' ties a fraction to its object like a bracket, so it is resolved before the result is divided or multiplied further.

3Use a² − b² for near-pairs

103 × 97 = 100² − 3². 52 × 48 = 50² − 2².

Why it worksNumbers equally far from a round number multiply to the square of the centre minus the square of the gap.

4Round to friendly numbers, then calculate

49.8 × 19.9 ≈ 50 × 20 = 1,000.

Why it worksRounding shifts each number by under 1%, while options in approximation questions usually differ by 5% or more.

5Rationalise with the conjugate

Multiply top and bottom by the same expression with the middle sign flipped.

Why it works(√a + √b)(√a − √b) = a − b, which removes the root from the denominator.

6Reverse BODMAS for a missing value

Undo the last operation first: undo + and −, then ÷ and ×.

Why it worksSolving is BODMAS run backwards, so the last step performed is the first undone.

7Pair up numbers that make round values

In 25 × 17 × 4 do 25 × 4 = 100 first, then 100 × 17 = 1,700.

Why it worksMultiplication does not depend on order, so grouping friendly pairs removes work.

8Squares of numbers ending in 5

For 35², compute 3 × 4 = 12 and append 25 to get 1,225.

Why it works(10a + 5)² = 100a(a + 1) + 25.

9Add surds only when they are alike

√12 + √3 = 2√3 + √3 = 3√3.

Why it worksOnly surds with the same root part can be added, so simplify each one first.

One-line method
Brackets, then 'of', then ÷ and × left to right, then + and − left to right; for approximation round first.
Solved examples

6 solved examples, from easy to tricky

The numbered circles in the question line match the red-pen steps below it.

Example 1 · Basic BODMAS
Simplify 18 + 2 × (5 + 3) − ¼ of 40
1Bracket first: 5 + 3 = 8, then 2 × 8 = 16.
2'Of' means multiply: ¼ × 40 = 10.
18 + 16 − 10 = 24.
Example 2 · Fractions
Simplify 3/4 of 48 ÷ 6 + 5
1'Of' first: 3/4 × 48 = 36.
2Then divide: 36 ÷ 6 = 6, then add 5.
6 + 5 = 11.
Example 3 · Surds
Simplify √12 × √3 + (√5)²
1√12 × √3 = √36 = 6.
2(√5)² = 5.
6 + 5 = 11.
Example 4 · Rationalise
Rationalise 1/(√5 − 2)
1Multiply top and bottom by the conjugate (√5 + 2).
2Denominator: (√5 − 2)(√5 + 2) = 5 − 4 = 1.
1/(√5 − 2) = √5 + 2.
Example 5 · Approximation
Find the approximate value of 39.8% of 601
1Round 39.8% to 40% and 601 to 600.
240% of 600 = 240.
The value is about 240 (exact value 239.198).
Example 6 · Powers and roots
Simplify (7² − 5²) ÷ √36 + 3 × 4
1Bracket first: 49 − 25 = 24, and √36 = 6.
2Then 24 ÷ 6 = 4 and 3 × 4 = 12.
4 + 12 = 16.
qa-03:
Percentage & Its Applications

Percentage is the single most-tested concept in CUET's numerical section because profit-loss, interest, discount and data-interpretation questions are all percentage in disguise.

Start here

What Percentage is about

Percentage means 'per hundred'. It is the common language behind profit and loss, interest, discount, population change and every data-interpretation chart. A student who is fast at percentages is fast at half of the numerical section.

The exam rarely asks for a plain percentage. It disguises it: a price that rises and then falls, a population that grows for two years, or a slice of a pie chart.

%means per 100
6core formulas
8fraction pairs to know
30–45 starget per question
At a glance

Topic map: the key ideas in one picture

The flow

The method, step by step

Follow the same order every time. Each step feeds the next, so you never have to hold the whole problem in your head.

1
Find the base

Identify the base, the quantity that counts as 100%: original price, total, or old value.

2
Convert to multipliers

Convert each percentage into a fraction or multiplier (20% = 1/5, +20% = ×1.2).

3
Apply changes in order

Apply the changes one after another, each on the latest value.

4
Compare with the base

Compare the final value with the base to get the net change.

5
Sanity-check the direction

Check the direction of the answer (increase or decrease) against common sense.

In depth

The ideas behind the topic, explained

Percent is a fraction in disguise

Every percentage is a fraction with denominator 100, so 35% is 35/100 = 7/20. Seeing 'x% of y' as a fraction lets you simplify before multiplying. Pairs such as 25% = 1/4 and 12.5% = 1/8 turn percentage work into division by small whole numbers.

Why successive changes multiply

If a value rises 10% it becomes 1.1 times itself; a further rise of 20% multiplies that new value by 1.2. The two changes act on different bases, so the net factor is 1.1 × 1.2 = 1.32, a 32% rise, not 30%. The same reasoning shows that +20% followed by −20% leaves 0.96 of the original, a 4% fall.

Percentage versus percentage points

A change from 40% to 50% is 10 percentage points, but it is a 25% rise in the percentage itself (10 ÷ 40). Exam options often include both versions, so check which one is wanted. Words such as 'points' or 'by how many percent' usually settle it.

The tricks

9 tricks, and why each one works

A trick you only memorise fails under pressure. Each one comes with its reason, so you can rebuild it if you forget it. Tap a trick to open it.

1Find the base first

Ask 'percent of what' and treat that quantity as 100%.

Why it worksEvery percentage question hides a base. The right method on the wrong base gives the wrong answer.

2Use multipliers, not steps

+20% is ×1.2 and −20% is ×0.8, so +20% then −20% is ×0.96, a 4% fall.

Why it worksA multiplier folds the whole change into one multiplication, so long chains become one line.

3Learn the fraction pairs

12.5% = 1/8, so 12.5% of 240 = 240 ÷ 8 = 30.

Why it worksA percentage becomes a division by a small whole number, which is quicker than decimal multiplication.

4Reverse percentage: divide, do not subtract

If a price after a 20% rise is 960, the original is 960 ÷ 1.2 = 800.

Why it worksThe 20% was taken on the original, so the final value is 120% of the original; undo it by dividing by 1.2.

5x% of y = y% of x

35% of 40 = 40% of 35 = 14.

Why it worksBoth equal x × y / 100, so choose whichever is easier.

6Percentage points are not percent

20% to 25% is 5 percentage points but 25% growth.

Why it worksPoints compare the two percentages directly; percent change compares them relative to the starting value.

7Use 10% as the building block

For 35% of 240 find 10% = 24, then 3.5 × 24 = 84.

Why it works10% is a single decimal shift, and other percentages are multiples of it.

8Compare using percentages

To compare 3/8 with 0.37, convert: 3/8 = 37.5%, which is larger than 37%.

Why it worksConverting both numbers to percentages puts them on a common scale.

9Percentage of a percentage

20% of 30% of 500 is 0.2 × 0.3 × 500 = 30.

Why it worksEach 'of' multiplies by the fraction, so chain the decimals.

Find the base → convert to a multiplier → apply each change on the latest value → compare with the base.

1Change = 100 − 80 = 20. The base is the OLD price, 80.

Example 3 · Successive change
A number is increased by 20% and then decreased by 20%
1Multiplier for +20% is 1.2; for −20% it is 0.8.

The net change is −4%, a 4% decrease.
Example 4 · Reverse percentage
After a 20% rise a price is ₹960. Find the original price
1The final price is 120% of the original: original × 1.2 = 960.
2Divide: 960 ÷ 1.2 = 800.
The original price was ₹800.
Example 5 · Votes
A candidate gets 45% of the votes and loses by 300 votes to the only other candidate. Find the total votes
1The winner has 55%, so the difference is 55% − 45% = 10% of the total.
210% of the total = 300, so the total is 3,000.
Total votes = 3,000.

1Girls playing chess = 25% of 60% = 0.25 × 0.60.
20.25 × 0.60 = 0.15.
15% of all students.

Profit, Loss & Discount

These questions test whether you can correctly identify the BASE (cost price vs marked price) before applying a percentage — the most common trap in this topic.

Start here

What Profit, Loss and Discount are about

Profit and loss compares what a seller paid (the cost price) with what the seller received (the selling price). Discount is the reduction from the marked price. The whole topic is percentages with one rule: profit and loss are always worked out on the cost price unless the question says otherwise.

The exam tests whether you choose the right base. A single wrong base turns a correct method into a wrong answer.

CPbase for profit and loss
MPbase for discount

1

Write down the cost price (CP), selling price (SP) and marked price (MP) if given.

2

Decide the base: CP for profit or loss, MP for discount.

3

If no amount is given, assume CP = 100 to keep percentages simple.

4

Apply SP = CP × (100 ± P%)/100 or the discount formula.

5

Check: profit means SP is greater than CP, loss means SP is less than CP.

In depth

The ideas behind the topic, explained

The base decides the answer

Profit and loss percentages are measured against the cost price, and discount against the marked price. Changing the base changes the answer even when the rupee amounts are the same. A profit of ₹20 on a cost of ₹100 is 20%, but the same ₹20 is only 16.67% of the selling price of ₹120.

The marked price is a bridge

Shopkeepers print a marked price above the cost price, then give a discount from it. The chain is cost price → mark-up → marked price → discount → selling price. Each arrow is a multiplier, so the whole chain is one multiplication, which is why 'marked 40% above cost, 25% discount' becomes 1.4 × 0.75 = 1.05.

Why equal gain and loss is a loss

Almost every question uses one of two formulas. The skill is choosing the right one and handling time in years, half-years or quarters correctly.

The ideas behind the topic, explained

Why compound interest grows faster

Simple interest always earns on the original principal, so each year adds the same amount. Compound interest adds each year's interest to the principal, so later years earn interest on earlier interest. After 2 years at 10% on ₹10,000 the extra comes from the ₹1,000 earned in year one, which itself earns ₹100 in year two.

The two-year shortcut

The difference between compound and simple interest for two years is P(R/100)². It equals exactly the interest earned on the first year's interest, which is why it needs no other information. For three years the difference is P(R/100)² × (3 + R/100).

Rates are quoted per year. If interest is compounded half-yearly, halve the rate and double the number of periods; for quarterly, divide the rate by 4 and multiply the periods by 4. In simple interest always convert months to years: 18 months is 1.5 years.

A ratio compares two quantities of the same kind (a : b). A proportion says two ratios are equal. An average is the single value that would replace every item if all items were equal: the sum divided by the number of items. The ideas behind the topic, explained

What a ratio really says

A ratio such as 3 : 5 fixes only the relative sizes: for every 3 units of one quantity there are 5 of the other. It is not a pair of actual amounts. To reach real amounts you need one extra piece of information, such as the total or the difference, which gives the value of one part.

The average is the value that would make all items equal while keeping the total. Items above it are balanced by items below it. That is why one extreme value pulls the average a lot, and why replacing a number changes the average by (change ÷ count).

In direct proportion both quantities rise together, so their ratio stays fixed (cost and quantity). In inverse proportion one rises as the other falls, so their product stays fixed (men and days). Identifying the direction first decides whether you set ratios equal or products equal.

The ideas behind the topic, explained

The idea behind an AP

In an AP each step adds the same amount d. So the nth term is the first term plus (n − 1) steps of d. Because the terms are evenly spaced, the average of the whole progression is the average of its first and last terms, which is why the sum is n times that average.

The idea behind a GP

In a GP each step multiplies by the same ratio r. Growth is therefore exponential: the nth term is a × r^(n−1). If |r| is less than 1 the terms shrink towards zero and the infinite sum settles at a/(1 − r); if |r| is 1 or more the sum does not settle.

Recognising each type fast

Subtract neighbouring terms; equal results mean an AP. Divide neighbouring terms; equal results mean a GP. Exam sequences often hide the type: 2, 6, 18 gives a ratio of 3 (GP) while 2, 6, 10 gives a difference of 4 (AP). Checking both takes seconds.

When a transversal cuts two parallel lines it makes eight angles but only two sizes: some equal x, the others equal 180° − x. In a right triangle the square of the hypotenuse equals the sum of the squares of the other two sides. Integer triples such as 3-4-5, 5-12-13, 8-15-17 and 7-24-25 appear repeatedly. Spotting a multiple of a triple gives the third side without calculation.

The ideas behind the topic, explained

Area measures a surface, volume measures space

Area counts unit squares that cover a surface, so it is measured in square units. Volume counts unit cubes that fill a solid, so it is in cubic units. The surface area of a solid is the total area of its outer faces, while capacity is the volume it can hold, measured in litres.

Where the formulas come from

A prism or cylinder is its base area times its height. A cone or pyramid has one third of that, because three of them fill the matching prism or cylinder. The sphere's volume (4/3)πr³ and surface area 4πr² come from slicing and unrolling it. Knowing these links makes recall easier.

Combined solids add their volumes; hollow solids subtract. When a solid is melted and recast, the volume stays constant, so equate the volumes. When every length is multiplied by k, areas scale by k² and volumes by k³.

Mean, Median & Mode

These three 'averages' answer different questions — mean is the arithmetic balance point, median is the middle value, mode is the most frequent value — and CUET often asks you to compute or compare all three for a small dataset.

Start here

What Mean, Median and Mode are about

Mean, median and mode are three ways of describing the 'centre' of a data set. The mean is the arithmetic balance point, the median is the middle value once the data is sorted, and the mode is the most frequent value.

CUET asks you to compute them for a small data set, to find a missing value from a given mean, or to see what happens to them when values are added, removed or changed.

6formulas and shortcuts

Follow the same order every time. Each step feeds the next, so you never have to hold the whole problem in your head.

1

2

Sort the data in ascending order (needed for the median and the mode).

3

Compute the mean = sum ÷ n.

4

Find the median: the middle value (odd n) or the average of the two middle values (even n).

5

In depth

The ideas behind the topic, explained

Three measures, three ideas of the centre

The mean uses every value, so it balances the data but is pulled by extremes. The median uses only position, so it is steady against extremes and best for skewed data such as incomes. The mode is the most common value and is the only measure that also works for categories such as favourite colours.

What changes when the data changes

Adding the same number to every value shifts the mean, median and mode by that number. Multiplying every value scales all three by that factor. Adding an extreme value moves the mean much more than the median. These rules answer many 'what happens if' questions without calculation.

Spread and grouped data

The range (largest minus smallest) is the simplest measure of spread. For a frequency table the mean uses Σfx ÷ Σf, where each value counts as many times as its frequency. The modal class is the class with the highest frequency.

The tricks

9 tricks, and why each one works

A trick you only memorise fails under pressure. Each one comes with its reason, so you can rebuild it if you forget it. Tap a trick to open it.

1Sort first, always

Write the data in order before finding the median or the mode.

Why it worksThe median is defined by position in the ordered list, so unsorted data gives a wrong middle.

2The median position is (n + 1)/2

For 7 values it is the 4th value; for 8 values, the average of the 4th and 5th.

Why it worksThe middle sits halfway through the list; with an even count there are two middle values.

3Work with sums for the mean

Sum = mean × count; new mean = new sum ÷ new count.

Why it worksA mean is a sum divided by a count, so changing the data changes the sum and the count.

4Shift and scale

Adding k to every value adds k to the mean; multiplying by k multiplies the mean by k.

Why it worksEvery value moves by the same rule, so their average moves by the same rule.

5The median resists outliers

One huge value pulls the mean but hardly moves the median.

Why it worksThe median depends only on position, whereas the mean uses the size of every value.

6Mode ≈ 3 × Median − 2 × Mean

Use it to estimate the third measure when two are known.

Why it worksIt is an empirical relation for moderately skewed data.

7Mean from deviations

Pick an assumed mean A; the mean = A + the average of (x − A).

Why it worksSmall deviations are easier to add than large values.

8Mean of the first n natural numbers

The mean is (n + 1)/2, so for 1 to 99 it is 50.

Why it worksThe sum is n(n + 1)/2, which is then divided by n.

9Combined mean

The ideas behind the topic, explained

Reading before calculating

Every chart has a title, axis labels, a legend and a unit. The title says what is measured, the axes say which category sits where, the legend decodes colours or shades, and the unit says whether numbers are in lakhs, thousands or per cent. Spending ten seconds here prevents the commonest DI error.

Choosing the right calculation

Most DI questions reduce to five calculations: a share (part ÷ whole), a change (difference ÷ old), a ratio, an average, or a total. Identify which one the question wants and extract only the needed numbers. Ignore the rest of the chart.

Estimation in DI

Options are normally spread apart, so approximate values are enough. Round the numbers, compute quickly, and pick the nearest option. Use exact calculation only when two options are very close, such as 24.5% and 25.0%.

2Use the pie chart's percentage directly
